claims.text: The target material is a multi-principal-element refractory high-entropy alloy.
Untreated refractory high-entropy alloys can form discontinuous, non-protective mixed oxides during high-temperature exposure.
The intervention is deposition of an approximately 50–100 nm alumina coating by atomic layer deposition.
ALD deposition will produce a dense, continuous, adherent alumina film on the alloy surface.
A continuous alumina surface film can improve the high-temperature oxidation resistance of a refractory high-entropy alloy.
The ALD alumina layer will act as a diffusion barrier that retards oxygen ingress.
Retarding oxygen ingress will limit formation of mixed, non-protective oxide scales.
Limiting oxygen ingress and non-protective scale formation will reduce oxidation kinetics.
At approximately 1200°C in air for 100 hours, the coating will remain effective.
Under the specified exposure, coated samples will have significantly lower oxidation-induced mass gain than untreated controls.
Under the specified exposure, coated samples will develop a more uniform and adherent oxide layer than untreated controls.
Untreated refractory high-entropy alloys typically exhibit high mass gain and rapid oxidation when their surface oxide is non-dense or non-protective.
Untreated refractory high-entropy-alloy oxide scales typically have poor adhesion.
Thermal-expansion mismatch may cause the alumina coating to delaminate and lose effectiveness.
Service conditions exceeding the alumina layer's thermal stability may degrade performance.
Coating performance may vary with alloy composition and microstructure.
Mass gain per unit area can be used to track high-temperature oxidation behavior.
Failure to obtain either a statistically significant mass-gain reduction or a continuous, adherent protective alumina-based layer would falsify the hypothesis.
